content: Wheatgrass is the young shoot of plants belonging to the genus Caroline, particularly Agropyron cristatum, which is closely related to wheat. Some wheatgrass products are also derived from Triticum aestivum, commonly known as wheat. The fresh leaf buds of wheatgrass can be juiced or dried into a powder, both of which are rich in chlorophyll, amino acids, minerals, vitamins, and enzymes. The unprocessed plant also contains dietary fiber, which supports colon health. The use of wheatgrass in Western diets began in the 1930s, spearheaded by Charles F. Schnabel, who sought to popularize its consumption. In the 1940s, Ann Wigmore further promoted wheatgrass, attributing its use to the remission of her cancer. Wigmore authored several books on the subject. Wheatgrass is typically consumed in doses of 5 grams (in powder or tablet form) or as a freshly squeezed 30 mL shot once daily. For therapeutic purposes, higher doses of 2–4 ounces may be taken 1–3 times per day on an empty stomach before meals. Some individuals increase their intake to 3–4 times daily for detoxification purposes. However, individuals with poor diets may experience nausea when consuming high doses of wheatgrass. Wheatgrass grown indoors under artificial conditions contains fewer nutrients compared to wheatgrass cultivated outdoors in natural environments. Outdoor wheatgrass, particularly that grown in regions known for winter wheat production (such as the breadbasket areas of the United States and Canada), is only available for a few days each year. Winter wheat requires over 200 days of slow growth in cold temperatures to achieve peak nutritional content. At this stage, the plant is only 7–10 inches tall due to its slow growth during the cold winter months in climates like the Midwestern United States, which are ideal for its development. In contrast, tray-grown wheatgrass, cultivated quickly indoors, produces thin, pale leaves with significantly lower nutritional content. The highest nutritional benefits are derived from wheatgrass grown under natural conditions and harvested at the optimal time of year when its nutritional value peaks. Most individuals seeking such high-quality wheatgrass opt for dehydrated powders and tablets produced by reputable companies that grow the plant organically in ideal climates, such as the Midwest. It is crucial that the wheatgrass be harvested before the jointing stage, which occurs for only a few days in winter wheat grown in breadbasket regions. Proponents of wheatgrass consumption claim that it provides numerous health benefits, including increased energy, body alkalization, improved digestion, cancer prevention, diabetes and heart disease prevention, relief from constipation, detoxification of heavy metals from the bloodstream, liver cleansing, prevention of hair loss, and support for managing menopause. However, these claims lack substantiation in scientific literature. Dr. Samir Samman has noted that none of these claims have been scientifically validated. One popular claim is that a single serving of wheatgrass is as nutritionally valuable as a kilogram of green vegetables. This assertion likely originates from Charles F. Schnabel, who reportedly stated that fifteen pounds of wheatgrass is equivalent to 350 pounds of the choicest vegetables. While this statement appears exaggerated, it was likely intended to emphasize the plant's perceived health benefits. Schnabel's research focused on wheatgrass grown outdoors in Kansas, where it underwent slow growth during the winter and was harvested at a specific time in early spring, known as the jointing stage. The wheatgrass was then dehydrated and processed into powders and tablets for human consumption. This process required 200 days of slow growth in Kansas's natural climate to achieve high nutritional levels. When grown naturally, wheatgrass develops a dense root structure and benefits from over 200 days of sunlight, resulting in a plant with exceptionally high nutritional value. Using Schnabel's research to promote wheatgrass grown rapidly in trays under artificial conditions is an invalid comparison. Wheatgrass grown quickly in trays for ten days under artificial conditions contains significantly less nutritional content than wheatgrass grown outdoors in climates like the Midwestern United States and Canada, harvested at the once-per-year jointing stage. Dehydrated wheatgrass powder, if grown organically under natural conditions and harvested before the jointing stage, has been shown to have a much higher nutritional value than fresh juice wheatgrass grown under artificial conditions. A single teaspoon of such powder is nutritionally equivalent to a USDA serving of spinach or other dark green vegetables. However, not all dehydrated wheatgrass products adhere to the standards established by Schnabel's research. The chlorophyll molecule in wheatgrass is structurally similar to hemoglobin, leading some to believe that wheatgrass supports blood flow, digestion, and overall detoxification. While no direct research links chlorophyll to blood-building, nutrients associated with dark green leafy vegetables are known to be important for healthy blood. Comparative analyses have demonstrated that dehydrated wheatgrass powder grown under natural conditions has a much higher nutritional value than wheatgrass juice grown in artificial hot-house environments. Ann Wigmore encouraged her students to dehydrate raw foods at low temperatures to preserve their nutrients. However, she inappropriately used Schnabel's scientific findings on dehydrated wheatgrass to support the rapid growth of wheatgrass under artificial conditions. In popular culture, wheatgrass has been referenced in various media. In the FX television series Nip/Tuck, Dr. Christian Troy grows and consumes wheatgrass in several episodes. In The Simpsons episode When You Dish Upon a Star, Homer invents a cocktail made of wheatgrass and vodka called a lawnmower. In another episode, Make Room for Lisa, Lisa is given a shot of wheatgrass juice, and her disgust at the taste is interpreted as a sign of its effectiveness. In Sex and the City, wheatgrass is mentioned as a remedy for altering the taste of bodily fluids.
